title: Kraft Heinz to divest its North American coffee business in $650 million deal
description: Robert Caplin | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesKraft Heinz announced Wednesday that it will divest its North American coffee unit in a deal that values the b
body: Robert Caplin | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesKraft Heinz announced Wednesday that it will divest its North American coffee unit in a deal that values the business at $650 million on an enterprise basis, as it works to refocus on its core brands. The deal with private equity firm One Rock Capital Partners includes brands such as Maxwell House and Gevalia and is expected to close in mid-2027, the company said in a news release. Kraft Heinz will retain a 30% noncontrolling equity stake in the business. Kraft Heinz said it will use the $500 million of post-tax cash proceeds from the transaction to pay down its debts as it works to prioritize resources where it can accelerate growth.  "This transaction is a meaningful step in unlocking value from our portfolio and will further accelerate the momentum behind our transformation," Steve Cahillane, CEO of Kraft Heinz, said in the release. Cahillane joined the company in January and called off plans to split the company in two, a move that would have reversed the blockbuster $46 billion merger from a decade ago. He said the problems Kraft Heinz faced were "fixable and within our control." The turnaround efforts have included a $700 million investment back into the business and a sharpened focus on some of its core brands. Also on Wednesday, Kraft Heinz reported third-quarter earnings that beat expectations and raised its 2026 outlook. It now expects organic net sales to be down 0.5% to 1.25%, an improvement from its second-quarter report, which projected that sales could decrease as much as 2%. "Our 2026 operating plan to turn around the U.S. business and accelerate growth internationally is on track," Cahillane said. "Relative to last year, our market share, sales, and volume trends are improving in every region. We are increasingly meeting consumers where they are, and giving them more reasons to choose our brands."Shares of the company were up about 5% Wednesday morning.

schema.headline: Kraft Heinz to divest its North American coffee business in $650 million deal

title: Private companies added 86,000 jobs in October, slightly higher than expected, ADP says
description: Jobseekers speak to recruiters at the NC4ME hiring event for military veterans in Wilmington, North Carolina, US, on Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. Allison
body: Jobseekers speak to recruiters at the NC4ME hiring event for military veterans in Wilmington, North Carolina, US, on Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. Allison Joyce | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesPrivate sector job growth held steady in October, with gains spread across sectors, as the labor market showed fresh signs of stabilization, ADP reported Wednesday.The payrolls processing firm said companies added 86,000 jobs during the month, the same as the downwardly revised total for September and slightly ahead of the Dow Jones estimate for 75,000.Employment gains came mainly in the service sector.Trade, transportation and utilities led with 39,000 new jobs, while education and health services added 28,000, and leisure and hospitality contributed 19,000. Other sectors showing gains included financial activities (15,000), construction (13,000) and other services (10,000).However, some of the gains were offset by a decline of 27,000 in professional and business services and a loss of 8,000 in natural resources and mining. Information services, a sector potentially impacted by the artificial intelligence buildout, lost 2,000 jobs.Salaries continued to show gains, particularly for those changing jobs — those workers saw a 4.8% annual gain. A report Tuesday from the Bureau of Labor Statistics showed that the number of people quitting their job, a sign of labor market mobility, hit its highest level since March 2025.Workers overall saw a 3.2% base pay gain, while gross pay increased 4.7% annually. Pay for those staying in their jobs rose 3%."Employers of all sizes were hiring last month, and our data suggests that job-changers were lured by a combination of bonuses, overtime, and more hours in addition to higher base pay," said ADP's chief economist, Nela Richardson. "Taken together, earnings growth for these workers hit its fastest pace since March 2024."Companies with between 50 and 499 workers added 33,000 jobs. Large businesses added 24,000, while small firms increased rolls by 28,000.The ADP report serves as a precursor to the BLS nonfarm payrolls count to be released Friday.Economists surveyed by Dow Jones are looking for the BLS report for October to show a gain of 59,000 after September's modest growth of 29,000.

schema.headline: Private companies added 86,000 jobs in October, slightly higher than expected, ADP says

title: CVS to split off drugstore business in major breakup of healthcare giant; shares fall 10%
description: CVS Health plans to split into two separate public companies by the first half 2028 in what would be one of the largest corporate splits in history, t
body: CVS Health plans to split into two separate public companies by the first half 2028 in what would be one of the largest corporate splits in history, the company announced Wednesday. The move would reverse the company's massive $78 billion acquisition of its insurer, Aetna, and dismantle the vertically integrated healthcare conglomerate it created in 2018. The plan would specifically separate CVS' roughly 9,000 retail pharmacies from its major insurance business and pharmacy benefit manager, Caremark, one of the nation's three largest PBMs.The decision follows a "comprehensive strategic review" by the company's board of directors, according to a news release. Shares of CVS fell roughly 10% on Wednesday after the announcement. It's a stunning reversal for the healthcare powerhouse, which has spent the last two decades working to turn itself into a one-stop health destination. The move also comes as CVS' aggressive turnaround plan under CEO David Joyner shows substantial progress, with the company pursuing $2 billion in cost cuts, store closures, leadership shakeups and efforts to rein in Medicare Advantage costs. "From a position of strength, and a focus on the long term, we plan to create two focused companies to improve consumer engagement, affordability, and care coordination," Joyner said in the release. A person walks into a CVS pharmacy near George Washington University in Washington, U.S., August 15, 2024. Kaylee Greenlee Beal | ReutersCVS shares have jumped roughly 70% since Joyner took the helm in October 2024, bringing the company's market value to $117 billion.The two new companies would both be publicly traded. The insurance and PBM company will retain the CVS Health name and be run by Joyner, while the other company will be called CVS Pharmacy and be led by Prem Shah, who is currently group president of CVS Health. Additional leadership positions and board members will be announced at a later date, CVS said. Existing CVS shareholders will own shares in both companies after the split. The Financial Times on Tuesday first reported the breakup plans.The company's pharmacy business raked in $37.66 billion in 2025 sales, while its insurance unit booked $36.29 billion in revenue and healthcare services segment generated $51.24 billion. CVS on Wednesday also posted third-quarter earnings and revenue that topped Wall Street expectations. Total sales climbed to $108.40 billion, from $102.87 billion in the prior-year period. Sales were boosted by year-over-year growth in the company's health care benefits and health services segments. Meanwhile, revenue in its pharmacy services business slid from the previous year. How the CVS split would workOn Wednesday, CVS said it will lump its insurer and PBM with its primary care business Oak Street Health, home-visit provider Signify Health and the company's specialty drug business. CVS also said the split will allow the two companies to experience a "focused strategic agenda" and greater ability to "innovate, adopt technology, increase efficiency," among other benefits. It's not the first time CVS has weighed splitting the company. In October 2024, CVS engaged advisors in a strategic review of its business and considered breaking up its retail pharmacy and insurance units. Even so, Leerink Partners analyst Michael Cherny said the split "feels like a complete shock" in a Tuesday note. But he said that the retail pharmacy business has been performing well, winning market share from competitors and seeing stabilizing gross margins thanks to CostVantage, a new pharmacy reimbursement model introduced by CVS last year. "In this context, perhaps the outlook for a standalone retail pharmacy (still with meaningful scale and leverage on its own) is stronger now than before," Cherny wrote. He added that "the rationale could also be to avoid what has been relentless state legislative scrutiny over the company's level of vertical integration." The potential breakup also comes as pharmacy benefit managers face mounting bipartisan scrutiny in Washington, D.C., and across states. PBMs, which negotiate drug prices and manage prescription drug benefits on behalf of insurers and employers, have been criticized for opaque pricing practices, their growing market power and potential conflicts of interest when they are owned by companies that also operate insurers and pharmacies. Congress enacted PBM reforms in February, including provisions to change how PBMs are compensated under Medicare Part D. Meanwhile, states have increasingly moved to restrict PBMs' ownership of pharmacies.

schema.headline: CVS to split off drugstore business in major breakup of healthcare giant; shares fall 10%

title: Wayfair sales jump 10% as furniture retailer says it's winning share of sluggish market
description: Cheng Xin | Getty ImagesWayfair on Wednesday said it posted its strongest quarter of sales growth since the pandemic as the furniture retailer continu
body: Cheng Xin | Getty ImagesWayfair on Wednesday said it posted its strongest quarter of sales growth since the pandemic as the furniture retailer continues to win over customers and take market share.The company said it saw double-digit revenue growth in the U.S., reaching about $3 billion, an 11.4% increase from the year prior. Still, international net revenue for the quarter decreased 2.3% year over year to $380 million.The report comes as the housing market remains sluggish. But the furniture and home goods retailer has reported consistent growth over the past year. CFO Kate Gulliver told CNBC that Wayfair's momentum is building as it takes market share."We see the overall consumer in the U.S. in this category, we think it's roughly flattish, and so that's our [market] share momentum continuing to build," Gulliver said. She added that shopper loyalty, the opening of new stores, the company's luxury furniture business and an emphasis on value has allowed the company to win more consumers. Customers are also continuing to spend, whether at the company's value prices or on the luxury side, she added."We've been highly promotional for the last few years, and the promotional activity this year is actually very consistent with last year," she said. "It maintains this sort of momentum on promotional activity this year."Here's how the company performed in its third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:Earnings per share: 93 cents adjusted vs. 79 cents expectedRevenue: $3.42 billion vs. $3.38 billion expectedFor the period ended Sept. 30, Wayfair reported net income of $62 million, or 45 cents per share, compared with a loss of $99 million, or a loss of 76 cents per share, the year prior. Total revenue grew 9.7% year over year, reaching $3.42 billion.The company said its active customers grew 4.7% year over year, reaching 22.2 million. It also saw a 12.2% increase in orders delivered during the quarter to about 11 million.As the company looks ahead to the holiday season and the fourth quarter, Gulliver said it's maintaining promotional activity similar to last year. She added that the company is confident that its range of prices and products will appeal to a broad base of consumers."We've seen that growth play out," Gulliver said. "We've seen that flow through to EBITDA, ultimately to net income positive this quarter, which is really another key piece in the story and the momentum here, so we feel very good about the quarter of the performance."

schema.headline: Wayfair sales jump 10% as furniture retailer says it's winning share of sluggish market

title: Euro zone inflation hits 4% for first time in three years as interest rate hike looms
description: Shoppers at Roemerberg square in Frankfurt, Germany, on Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026. Ben Kilb | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesInflation in the euro area jumped
body: Shoppers at Roemerberg square in Frankfurt, Germany, on Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026. Ben Kilb | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesInflation in the euro area jumped to a three-year high of 4% in October, a flash estimate showed on Wednesday. The reading is in line with the expectations of economists polled by Reuters and was up from 3.8% in September. Officials said the increase was largely due to surging energy costs, with energy inflation rising to 20.8% from 18.9% in September. Europe, a net energy importer, is vulnerable to external energy shocks and has seen prices rise steadily since the start of the Iran war.October marked the first time inflation in the euro zone has hit or exceeded the 4% threshold since Sept. 2023's reading of 4.3%. Inflation also varied across the 21 euro zone economies, with Lithuania recording the hottest inflation rate of 6.1% while Malta's was the lowest at 2.3%. All euro zone countries saw inflation hold above the European Central Bank's 2% target. The euro was up 0.6% against the U.S. dollar on Wednesday morning, although the greenback fell against a basket of major currencies as counting continued in the U.S. midterm elections, while the yield on the 10-year German bund — broadly seen as a benchmark for euro zone bonds — was marginally higher.Policymakers said underlying inflation and wages were broadly stable, despite inflation sitting at a three-year high.  Rate hike looms — but French turmoil could complicate policyThe European Central Bank kept its key interest rate at 2.5% last month, following a hike of 25 basis points in September. Shortly before Wednesday's inflation print, markets were pricing in a 71.8% chance of a hike at the ECB's final meeting of the year in December. Following the data release, markets were pricing in more than a 72% chance of rates rising. Robert Mertens, global capital markets senior analyst at Validus Risk Management, cautioned that "ongoing turmoil in the French bond market is placing constraints on ECB policy" and the bank's capacity to get inflation under control. "Should we see an easing in French political unrest, the ECB could potentially pursue a more aggressive hiking path," he said. "If the ECB can deploy more aggressive tightening relative to the Federal Reserve, we would see increased Euro support and upside versus the Dollar."

schema.headline: Euro zone inflation hits 4% for first time in three years as interest rate hike looms

title: McDonald's stock rises as earnings beat, U.S. restaurants show improvement
description: McDonald's logo sign is seen in Berlin, Germany, on September 12, 2026. Marcin Golba | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesMcDonald's on Wednesday reported mixed q
body: McDonald's logo sign is seen in Berlin, Germany, on September 12, 2026. Marcin Golba | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesMcDonald's on Wednesday reported mixed quarterly results as traffic to its U.S. restaurants fell, leading to a slight decline in domestic same-store sales.The fast-food giant reported a 0.2% decrease in sales at its U.S. restaurants that have been open at least 13 months. Even so, the segment performed better than the 0.5% decline that Wall Street anticipated, according to a survey of analysts by StreetAccount."In the U.S., we're encouraged by improvement as the quarter progressed following our intervention on value," McDonald's CEO Chris Kempczinski said in a statement.McDonald's same-store sales returned to growth in September after falling in July and August, CFO Ian Borden said on the company's earnings conference call. However, in response to an analyst question, he clarified that he did not say that U.S. same-store sales would be better in the fourth quarter.Kempczinski said in August that the company's U.S. business was falling short on execution, particularly on the implementation of its value offerings. Like many restaurants, McDonald's has leaned into discounts to attract budget-conscious diners over the last two years.To reverse same-store sales declines, McDonald's focused its marketing on its Extra Value Meals and restarted regional and national promotions on its mobile app, which are important to its most frequent diners.As McDonald's tries to regain its footing in the U.S., the chain is also testing two new value menus, one with mix and match bundles and the other with set combinations of menu items, executives said on the earnings call. The offering that resonates the most with customers and franchisees will be rolled out across the U.S. in early 2027.Shares of the company rose about 5% in morning trading. Here's what the company reported compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:Earnings per share: $3.57 adjusted vs. $3.38 expectedRevenue: $7.16 billion vs. $7.29 billion expectedThe company reported third-quarter net income of $2.49 billion, or $3.51 per share, up from $2.28 billion, or $3.18 per share, a year earlier. Excluding restructuring charges and other items, McDonald's earned $3.57 per share.Net revenue rose 1% to $7.16 billion.The company's same-store sales rose 1.5%, lifted by its international segments. That topped analysts' expectations of a 1.3% increase, according to StreetAccount.McDonald's international developmental licensed markets business, which includes Japan and China, reported same-store sales growth of 4.2%. Wall Street was forecasting same-store sales to rise 2.1% for the division, based on StreetAccount estimates.The company's international operated division, which includes top markets like Australia and Germany, saw same-store sales growth of 1.4%. Still, the business underperformed Wall Street's expectations. Analysts were projecting same-store sales would rise 2.1%, according to StreetAccount. "In the majority of our large international markets, we're holding or gaining share," Borden said on the company's conference call. "It's a soft consumer environment, but we're doing well."France was a weak spot, McDonald's said. Kempczinski said that franchisees in France recently voted on a strategy to turn the business around. In addition to a softer economy in the country, McDonald's has also seen short-term disruptions related to student protests.

schema.headline: McDonald's stock rises as earnings beat, U.S. restaurants show improvement

title: Sen. Chris Murphy still hospitalized after suffering a stroke over the weekend
description: Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., talks with reporters during votes in the U.S. Capitol on Sept. 30, 2026.Tom Williams | CQ-Roll Call, Inc. | Getty ImagesSe
body: Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., talks with reporters during votes in the U.S. Capitol on Sept. 30, 2026.Tom Williams | CQ-Roll Call, Inc. | Getty ImagesSen. Chris Murphy remained hospitalized Tuesday after suffering a stroke over the weekend, his office confirmed."He's continuing to improve and heartened by the outpouring of well wishes," Josh Sorbe, Murphy's communications director, told CNBC in an emailed statement. "He early voted in Connecticut, and he encourages everyone to make their voices heard today by voting and sending a message in this defining election."His office did not offer additional details when asked about his status or his expected recovery.The Senate is due back in session Monday following Tuesday's midterm elections.Murphy began experiencing stroke symptoms on Saturday while at his son's hockey game, his chief of staff Allison Herwitt said in a statement Sunday."He was taken to a local hospital, where it was discovered he had experienced a stroke. He was transferred to Johns Hopkins for further monitoring and is responding well to treatment," Herwitt said. Herwitt said at the time that Murphy was "awake and alert."Johns Hopkins Hospital's main campus is in Baltimore, though it has other locations in and around Washington.Murphy is not up for reelection on Tuesday but had been traveling extensively this fall in support of Democratic candidates. Murphy came to the Senate in 2013 after a six-year stint in the U.S. House. He's also been mentioned as a potential 2028 presidential candidate.

schema.headline: Sen. Chris Murphy still hospitalized after suffering a stroke over the weekend

title: 10-year Treasury yield is little changed as traders mull over Democrats' midterm victories
description: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) during morning trading on Aug. 24, 2026 in New York City.Angela Weiss | AFP | Getty Im
body: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) during morning trading on Aug. 24, 2026 in New York City.Angela Weiss | AFP | Getty ImagesThe 10-year Treasury yield traded near the flatline on Wednesday as investors weighed big wins from Democrats in the U.S. midterm elections.The benchmark 10-year Treasury note yield was up less than 1 basis point at 4.954%. The 30-year bond yield advanced 1 basis point to 5.334%, and the shorter-term 2-year note yield added 1 basis point to 4.627%.One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely to one another.Democrats obtained majorities in both the House and Senate. Democrats flipped Senate seats from Republicans in Iowa, Kansas, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina, Maine and Texas. They also won key gubernatorial races in Ohio and Texas.The resounding victory by Democrats could rein in government spending from the Trump administration, as it makes it harder for the White House to push legislation through Congress. Traders at JPMorgan said one of the issues Wall Street is focusing on after the midterms is "reduced deficit spending.""This can be achieved by asserting power over the budget and likely wading through a government shutdown," they said.

schema.headline: 10-year Treasury yield is little changed as traders mull over Democrats' midterm victories

title: Analysis: The Democrats have one chance to extract concessions from Trump. Markets will hate it
description: U.S. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) speaks as House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY) looks on during a news conference at the U.S.
body: U.S. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) speaks as House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY) looks on during a news conference at the U.S. Capitol on January 08, 2026 in Washington, DC. Kevin Dietsch | Getty ImagesThe electoral sweep by Democrats on Tuesday night injects a new, unstable dynamic into the single biggest political risk to financial markets in the coming year: the debt limit. Unless a defeated Republican Party makes a swift and unlikely show of unity to take the issue off the table in its last few weeks in power, the protracted fight that will unfold is set to be nastier than ever, adding volatility to an already shaky bond market.Past episodes of brinkmanship around the need to raise the government's borrowing limit have involved Republicans in Congress demanding budget cuts from a Democratic president as the price of their vote. This time it will almost certainly be the left seeking concessions from the right. The debt limit is the definition of a must-pass bill, even more than issues like funding the government and the defense budget. That makes it potentially the one real chance the new Democratic majority in Congress has to extract concessions from a president who is already pledging to veto their agenda. Markets will hate the entire process, even if — as many expect — it ends in compromise. Because it is Democrats who hold the leverage, unlike past episodes, the ultimate agreement is more likely to increase government spending than lower it. With high bond yields weighing on the economy, and Americans expecting action from a newly empowered Democratic opposition, the fight could be particularly damaging. Many in the markets are stuck on the outdated idea that Democrats are less assertive than Republicans, said Aniket Shah, head of the Washington policy team at the investment bank Jefferies. "They have this sort of mental image of Biden-Harris 2024," said Shah. "I don't think they realize how aggressively Democrats plan to take 2027."Read more CNBC economics coverageAnalysis: Kevin Warsh is keeping Wall Street guessing. It may be his most powerful tool.Fed officials are already saying they’ll need to get back to hiking ratesPrivate companies added 86,000 jobs in October, slightly higher than expected, ADP saysTreasury's Bessent says ‘not necessarily’ a mistake if the Fed hikes againThe debt ceiling is a quirk of the congressional budgeting process. It stops the government from borrowing funds that Congress has already ordered federal agencies to spend. And because Congress has run deficits for decades — this year at $1.99 trillion — the pile of debt periodically bumps into the debt ceiling.Congress last set the limit in 2025, when it gave the Treasury Department the authority to borrow $41.1 trillion. The Treasury is likely to hit its maximum borrowing capacity by midsummer, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center, a nonprofit that tracks the issue. The Treasury can use budgeting techniques to extend the so-called X-date, when the U.S. would no longer be able to meet all its obligations, to sometime in the fourth quarter of 2027, according to Wall Street estimates. A few technical hiccups aside, the U.S. has never meaningfully breached the debt limit. The results of the U.S. missing payments would be chaotic as damage ripples out across the financial system into the global economy. U.S. default would immediately call into question trillions in Treasury securities that are the lifeblood of the global financial system. Damaging them could send the U.S. and global economies into an economic tailspin with no obvious means of recovery. Because the stakes are so high, Shah and many others on Wall Street have come to believe that the episode will produce volatility but will ultimately be resolved in compromise.Fights under former Presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden saw Republican congressional majorities use the issue to ram through spending reductions. (The 2025 raise was less contentious, because Republicans held Congress and the presidency. It was passed along party lines.) Still, the risk-taking in those episodes contributed to ratings firms' decisions to downgrade U.S. debt — and could again.President Donald Trump has called for Republicans to resolve the issue in the next few weeks, before the new Democratic-majority Congress is seated.That isn't likely. The 2025 debt limit increase only passed because it was tied to a package of tax cuts and other policy changes. Republican debt hawks complained but held their noses. Republicans may attempt to raise the limit in the coming lame-duck session under a budgeting procedure called reconciliation, which would allow them to move ahead without Democrats' votes. But success would require unity among a fractured, fleeting Republican majority that also faces several other more pressing priorities.The most likely path toward raising the debt limit is the incoming Democratic majority negotiating another temporary fix with Trump. But they aren't going to make it easy. The president has occasionally made noises about making deals, but the political incentives ahead of the 2028 presidential election are for both sides to dig in. "[Democrats] are going to want to embarrass the White House, and they're going to want to get leverage," Shah said. Democrats will use that to push to reverse cuts to Medicaid spending passed in 2025 and to try to restore healthcare spending, he said. Democrats could also seek to tie the debt limit to restraining signature Trump policies, such as limiting the war in Iran or rolling back tariffs, analysts at Goldman Sachs said in a research note Wednesday.Another potential compromise being considered in some corners of Washington is for Democrats to tie an increase in the corporate tax rate to a debt-limit raise, said George Pollack, senior U.S. analyst with Signum Global Advisers. Trump has shown he can be surprisingly flexible on similar issues, Pollack noted. That is what will make this debt-limit fight different. In the past, Republicans used it to try to win spending reductions they couldn't get through regular budget negotiations. Now Democrats will broaden it out into an all-purpose hostage. That effort is far more likely to raise overall government spending than cut it. "There's a very weird irony here," said Robert Sockin, chief U.S. economist at PGIM, an asset manager.The path to compromise will likely be rocky. Sockin believes it may turn out like the 2025 government shutdown. That was the longest government-wide shutdown in history, even though Democrats weren't in control of either house of Congress. This time they will have even more power.If the fight extends beyond the X-date, missing debt payments could do serious damage to the financial system. "It's not our base case, but we think the risk is higher than ever that you could get a technical default from the government," Sockin said. That would see the U.S. miss a payment, even if the government eventually makes it up.That would still hurt. "You'll get more downgrades to the U.S. sovereign, and those might bite more this time," Sockin said. Yields on longer-term Treasuries would rise to account for added uncertainty. Crossing the red line could prompt a "very negative reaction in equity markets," he said.The coming months will show just how close Democrats are willing to get to that line.

schema.headline: Analysis: The Democrats have one chance to extract concessions from Trump. Markets will hate it

title: Blood banks targeted in latest European fridge cyberattacks
description: Close up of the hands of a nurse from the French Blood Establishment holding blood collection tubes intended to receive blood samples during a plasma
body: Close up of the hands of a nurse from the French Blood Establishment holding blood collection tubes intended to receive blood samples during a plasma donation session at the Maison du Don in Saint Brieuc Cotes d Armor Brittany France on July 28, 2026. Helene Rigny | Afp | Getty ImagesFrench blood banks were on Monday affected by the recent wave of cybersecurity attacks on European refrigeration systems, the French Blood Establishment confirmed on Wednesday.The organization said that while it wasn't the direct target of the attack, cold storage units operated by external providers containing the EFS' blood products were compromised across three of its sites, with hackers cranking up temperatures. "Specifically, temperature and defrost thresholds were set to excessively high levels," the EFS said in a statement translated from French to English by CNBC. "These cold storage units—located at EFS preparation and distribution sites—are used to store blood products prior to their delivery to healthcare facilities, as well as samples intended for EFS biobanks."They also stored frozen plasma used for transfusions the manufacturing of medicinal products.The EFS said that its surveillance systems were triggered rapidly, and depending on the situation, affected equipment was either brought under control with no impact on the products or samples, or they were taken offline. No samples or blood products were lost during the attack, with samples quickly transferred to other facilities, the EFS added. The EFS is now coordinating with the French National Cybersecurity Agency (ANSSI) and the Ministry of Health and has increased monitoring of its equipmentHundreds of supermarkets across France and other European countries, including Belgium, Sweden and Finland, had their fridges remotely hacked and temperatures raised, resulting in potentially millions of euros of spoiled food."Several regional facilities of the French Blood ​Establishment (EFS) were affected by a cybersecurity incident ​that impacted certain cold storage room monitoring and control ‌systems," The situation is now under control and is being closely monitored, the French Health Ministry said in a statement, according to Reuters. They added that the safety of the blood supplies was ​preserved "thanks ​to the ⁠facilities' monitoring and alarm systems, as well as precautionary measures immediately ​implemented."

schema.headline: Blood banks targeted in latest European fridge cyberattacks

title: AI data center stocks and Musk's SpaceX decline as Texas governor result raises risks of a slowdown
description: State Rep. Gina Hinojosa, the 2026 Democratic nominee for Texas governor, speaks at an Arlington, Texas, campaign rally on Sunday, Sept. 27, 2026. She
body: State Rep. Gina Hinojosa, the 2026 Democratic nominee for Texas governor, speaks at an Arlington, Texas, campaign rally on Sunday, Sept. 27, 2026. She faces Gov. Greg Abbott, a Republican, in the Nov. 3 general election. (Eleanor Dearman/Fort Worth Star-Telegram/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)Eleanor Dearman | Fort Worth Star-Telegram | Getty ImagesAI data center stocks came under pressure as Democrats — seen as proponents of moratoriums on the buildout — won big in midterm elections and in key technology hubs like Texas.Markets were already anticipating the Democrats to win the House of Representatives and possibly take Senate control. But the Texas governor mansion going to Democrats was a big blow, analysts said. Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who wants to enact an immediate moratorium on data centers in the state, won over incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott. According to Wells Fargo, 27% of planned data center gigawatts is in the Lone Star State. The midterm elections will slow the pace of data center buildouts across the U.S., Dan Ives, partner at Yorkville Ives & Co., said in a note on Wednesday morning."There is no way to sugarcoat that Democrats taking control especially over the Senate will create some major hurdles for AI and tech legislation in the Beltway over the next 2 years," he said.He added that the election in Texas was the "biggest worry" of the night for tech investors and the AI trade because that's where around 25%-30% of data center gigawatts and capacity will come from.Shares of Elon Musk's SpaceX were down 4% after the open, and Tesla shares were down 5%. The Democrats' victory in Texas is a big setback for Musk, where he heavily backed Republican candidates, and where his companies Tesla and SpaceX are based. Musk spent a record of at least $474 million on the midterms and funneled $224 million into Texas alone, where Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton and Gov. Greg Abbott lost to Democrats. SpaceX is currently building out multiple gigawatts of data center capacity, including projects in Texas."Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Musk said in a post on X in the early hours on Wednesday, referring to his speculative plans to build AI infrastructure off-planet.Neoclouds CoreWeave and Iren fell by 4% in morning trading on Wednesday. Peer Nebius Group was down about 0.5% and Oracle was up 2%. Nvidia shares were slightly in the red.Tech giants Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft mostly bucked the trend and were higher. Alphabet was up 3%, Amazon was up 7%, Meta was up 2%, and Microsoft was up 5.5%.The Democratic win in Texas adds to existing pressure on the bull-market-leading AI trade. The Nasdaq-100 index fell into correction territory to end October as concerns mounted that the growth of data center spending by big hyperscalers and private AI juggernauts OpenAI and Anthropic was slowing."We believe the equity market reaction from the midterms mostly depends on the outcome of the Texas governor's race — a Dem win could potentially be a left-tail event to the AI trade, warned Ohsung Kwon, Wells Fargo's chief equity strategist, in a report this week.Democrats won or retained the governorships in other key data center states Georgia, Pennsylvania and Ohio. Georgia represents 7% of all the planned U.S. datacenter gigawatts, while Ohio and Pennsylvania account for 5% apiece, estimates Wells Fargo.Notable investment strategist Michael Hartnett of Bank of America warned earlier this year that Democrats winning the Senate, combined with taking the Texas governorship could lead to a "big slump" in stocks of more than 10% into year-end."Data centers went from being a popular economic development tool in 2024 and 2025 to something of a pariah by the time the midterm campaigns gathered steam," wrote the Washington policy team at Optimal Advisory this week. "The midterms are likely to send a message to local and state officials that there is a political upside to blocking, delaying and/or raising the cost of data centers."

title: SpaceX signs deal with Qualcomm to provide network technology for U.S. mobile service
description: watch nowSpaceX announced a deal with chipmaker Qualcomm to provide key network technology for Elon Musk's Starlink Mobile service, a challenger to Ve
body: watch nowSpaceX announced a deal with chipmaker Qualcomm to provide key network technology for Elon Musk's Starlink Mobile service, a challenger to Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile. Qualcomm said on Wednesday that the terrestrial network it will help SpaceX build will "complement Starlink's satellite capabilities," with a planned rollout to begin next year. Financial terms of the multiyear deal weren't disclosed."Together with SpaceX, we are building world-leading cellular infrastructure in the United States, advancing 5G today, with an opportunity to lay the foundation for AI-native 6G in the years ahead," Durga Malladi, an executive vice president at Qualcomm, said in the statement. Starlink is a critical piece of SpaceX's business, accounting for 36% of the company's revenue in the third quarter and 85% of its operating profit. But to date, the company's consumer business has been limited when it comes to mobile direct-to-device services as its satellite network can't provide all the voice, video and data coverage that competitors offer on popular smartphones. Now SpaceX is snapping up spectrum and forging partnerships to take on the major mobile carriers. Last month, the company announced an agreement to purchase a nationwide spectrum portfolio in the 800 MHz band. The news sent shares of U.S. carriers reeling. Earlier this week, the Washington Post reported that SpaceX is in talks to acquire EchoStar's Boost Mobile.SpaceX went public in June in the largest IPO on record and is now valued at close to $2 trillion.watch nowWith Qualcomm, SpaceX will be using the chipmaker's Dragonwing cellular infrastructure hardware and software in base stations to enable high-capacity coverage for Starlink Mobile.Qualcomm has a long history of making chips for cellular networks, but is best known for making the modems and radios that go inside devices, not base stations for running a wireless network. The company has targeted carriers and other infrastructure companies since it made a bigger push into the 5G infrastructure market in 2020.SpaceX represents one of Qualcomm's highest-profile customers or partners in 5G infrastructure, following earlier deals with Verizon, Dish, and Europe's Vodafone. While SpaceX plans to use Qualcomm's technology to establish tens of thousands of new cell sites, it hasn't announced partners among cell tower companies or said how many new towers may be required. Mobile carriers generally lease space from companies such as American Tower and Crown Castle, which commonly host multiple carriers from one site.SpaceX did not respond to CNBC's request for additional information.-- CNBC's Kif Leswing contributed reporting. title: Uber beats on revenue even as mobility and delivery units miss estimates
description: watch nowUber reported revenue for the third quarter that topped analysts' estimates, but the company missed expectations in its two key businesses.He
body: watch nowUber reported revenue for the third quarter that topped analysts' estimates, but the company missed expectations in its two key businesses.Here's how the company did versus analysts' estimates compiled by LSEG:Earnings per share: 25 cents vs. 96 cents expectedRevenue: $14.77 billion vs. $14.69 billion expectedRevenue increased 10% from $13.47 billion a year earlier. The company reported net income of $512 million, down 92% from a year earlier, when the company had a $4.9 billion benefit from a tax valuation release.Uber's core mobility unit, which is its ride-hailing service, saw a 2% decline in revenue to $7.52 billion, missing the average estimate of $7.71 billion, according to StreetAccount. Revenue in the food delivery business increased 23% to $5.49 billion, trailing the $5.51 billion average estimate.Total bookings of $59.82 billion were about in line with the $59.83 billion average analyst estimate, according to StreetAccount.Uber's revenue beat was due to growth in its freight division. Sales jumped 34% to $1.76 billion, topping the StreetAccount consensus of $1.49 billion,Read more CNBC tech newsElon Musk's record election bet backfired. The backlash may reach beyond one billionaireApple warns of risks related to AI agents behaving in 'unintended or unpredictable' waysAMD's data center revenue nearly doubles and Lisa Su expects growth to accelerateGoogle responds to political backlash over removing search from schools that ban AIUber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said, in prepared remarks ahead of a scheduled call, that the company's core mobility segment performed slightly below expectations overseas. "Elevated fuel prices and tighter driver availability weighed on supply growth in several international markets," he said, adding that Uber is making "targeted investments to strengthen driver supply."The company plans to have over 2,000 automated vehicles available on its platform by the end of 2027, half operating in the U.S. and half internationally. It expects to have around 700 available on its platform by the end of the year, adding Amazon's Zoox and Motional robotaxis to its platform in Las Vegas this quarter.Uber is also growing its delivery business through acquisitions of Delivery Hero in Germany and ezCater in the U.S. In its Uber Eats business, a recently expanded partnership with Costco in the U.S. is "tracking ahead of expectations," Khosrowshahi said. The company said Costco is now one of its top merchants in terms of gross bookings.For the fourth quarter, Uber sees overall bookings of $64.5 billion at the mid-point of its forecast, in line with the average StreetAccount estimate of $64.26 billion. title: CrowdStrike launches AI kill switch that it says can stop internal agents that go rogue
description: George Kurtz, CEO and founder of CrowdStrike, speaks to the Economic Club of New York in New York City, U.S., Oct. 23, 2025.  Brendan McDermid | Reute
body: George Kurtz, CEO and founder of CrowdStrike, speaks to the Economic Club of New York in New York City, U.S., Oct. 23, 2025.  Brendan McDermid | ReutersCrowdStrike is betting that it has a solution to rogue artificial intelligence. The cybersecurity vendor on Tuesday launched an AI kill switch designed to let security teams stop internal AI agents that go rogue, block them from relaunching and cut off their enterprise network access. The tool is built into CrowdStrike's Falcon Guardian platform, launched in September to secure AI agents. CrowdStrike also announced an integration with Anthropic's Claude Cowork."Having the ability to control and turn off, and make a decision and decide, I think that's really important for this next chapter of AI adoption," Chief Business Officer Daniel Bernard told CNBC.A string of recent high-profile cyber incidents has added urgency to calls for some kind of emergency shutdown mechanism. The Hugging Face breach orchestrated by rogue OpenAI agents in July was particularly alarming for businesses. Last week, Binance disclosed the largest crypto cyberattack on record and hackers have recently targeted hundreds of refrigerators and freezers at supermarkets in France.Over the summer, U.S. representatives introduced bipartisan legislation that would require AI companies to build shutdown capabilities into their models.Critics argue, however, that an emergency stop button is far too complicated to implement across multiple systems, data centers and complex AI models.Read more CNBC tech newsElon Musk's record election bet backfired. The backlash may reach beyond one billionaireApple warns of risks related to AI agents behaving in 'unintended or unpredictable' waysAMD's data center revenue nearly doubles and Lisa Su expects growth to accelerateGoogle responds to political backlash over removing search from schools that ban AIBernard said the kill switch operates like a circuit breaker in systems where customers use its Falcon platform. The process can detect internal agent activity but requires a human to decide to cut the agent off and reinstate access."If you kill a process at the root, and we have that level of access at the root … it's very binary," Bernard said. "You either kill the AI and the agent, or you don't, and then you report on that."The kill switch doesn't delete the agent's code but uses connected AI gateways to cut off access to the AI models that influence decisions, CrowdStrike said. In the age of AI, businesses are moving quickly to adopt autonomous tools, often without the necessary safeguards and protections. CrowdStrike believes its new tool will let companies stop AI agent 'misbehavior in its tracks, while leaving room for innovation. The company also announced plans to acquire AI observability startup Fiddler AI and AI security testing firm Dreadnode.CrowdStrike and its rivals are rapidly scooping up cybersecurity startups to keep up with increasing security demands. The need for AI security tools has also powered a broader wave of cybersecurity deal-making. watch now

title: U.S. midterm elections in pictures: Democrats' sweeping victories deliver rebuke to Trump
description: Democrats scored sweeping victories in the U.S. midterm elections on Wednesday, flipping key Republican-held seats in Congress and securing historic w
body: Democrats scored sweeping victories in the U.S. midterm elections on Wednesday, flipping key Republican-held seats in Congress and securing historic wins in traditionally conservative states, as voters delivered a setback to President Donald Trump.The party was projected to gain control of both chambers of Congress, with victories across several battleground states threatening to constrain Trump's legislative agenda for the remaining two years of his presidency.Here are some of the scenes from polling stations, campaign headquarters and election-night celebrations across the United States.Heading to the pollsVoters cast their ballots inside a polling location at the Bridge of Hope Church on November 3, 2026 in Youngstown, Ohio. Americans go to the polls in consequential midterm elections, where control of the House and the Senate is at stake for the remainder of President Donald Trump's second term in office.Jeff Swensen | Getty Images News | Getty Images Election workers celebrate as balloons are dropped when the polls closed at the Registrar of Voters in Kearny Mesa.The San Diego Union-tribune | Medianews Group | Getty ImagesTexasRepublican Senate candidate, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton speaks at a midterm election night watch party at the Westin Galleria Dallas after conceding to his opponent, Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico.Adam Gray | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesAmong the biggest surprises was Texas, where Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton to become the state's first Democratic U.S. senator since 1988. Fellow Democrat Gina Hinojosa also unseated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, becoming the state's first Latina governor and ending more than three decades of Republican control of the office.Supporters cheer during a  midterm election night watch party for Texas Democratic Senate candidate, State Rep. James Talarico at the Long Center on Nov. 3, 2026 in Austin, Texas. Brandon Bell | Getty ImagesPeople watching results on a screen during a midterm election night watch party. Paxton conceded the race to Democrat,  state Rep. Talarico.Adam Gray | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesNorth CarolinaDemocrat senatorial candidate Roy Cooper and his wife Kristin Cooper celebrate victory during an election night event in Raleigh, North Carolina.A.m Stewart | Afp | Getty ImagesIn North Carolina, former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper flipped a Republican-held Senate seat after defeating Trump-backed Michael Whatley. Cooper will succeed retiring Republican Sen. Thom Tillis, who announced his departure after clashing with Trump over his tax and spending legislation.GeorgiaSenator Jon Ossoff, a Democrat from Georgia, arrives for an election night event in Atlanta.Bloomberg | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesIn Georgia, Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff secured reelection against Trump-backed Republican Mike Collins, while former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms won the governor's race, becoming the first Black woman elected governor of a U.S. state.Representative Mike Collins, a Republican from Georgia and U.S. Senate candidate, during an election night event in Atlanta. Democratic Sen. Ossoff secured reelection against Trump-backed Republican Collins.Bloomberg | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesMeanwhile, in Ohio, former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown staged a political comeback, defeating Republican incumbent Jon Husted in a closely watched Senate race. The elections were widely viewed as a referendum on Trump's second term, with concerns over the cost of living, inflation and the war in Iran weighing on voter sentiment.—CNBC's Danielle DeVries contributed to this article.
